messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nadia Haddad is a 63-year-old Lebanese American woman who has worked for many years as an auditor, a job she once valued for its order, predictability, and reliance on careful observation. She came to treatment after months of worsening sleep, increasing constriction in her daily life, and a growing sense that her own reactions were no longer under her control. The event she returns to began during what was supposed to be a simple day trip with her younger niece, whom she had helped raise and regarded almost like a daughter. They had driven to a wooded state park outside the city, a place her niece had wanted to visit for the trails and quiet. Near the end of the afternoon, Nadia became separated from her when her niece went ahead down a path. What happened next is what still comes back to Nadia in a way that feels not like recollection but like being dropped back into the same moment. She remembers the trees, the smell of dirt and wet leaves, the muffled stillness of the area, then the abrupt wrongness of finding her niece trapped and injured in a small locked maintenance shed near the trail, panicked and calling out. Nadia remembers the metal door that would not give, the enclosed space, her niece’s terror, and her own frantic, useless attempts to open it before help arrived too late.

Since then, reminders do not come to Nadia as distant images. She describes them as arriving “all at once,” with the sounds, smell, visual detail, and bodily panic returning together so completely that for a few moments she is certain she is there again. The terror is the same terror: her heart pounds, her chest tightens, and she feels herself become physically braced before she has even had time to think. What unnerves her most is how suddenly it happens. She can be moving through an ordinary day and something in the environment will pull the whole scene back without warning. A locked conference room at work, a small records archive with no easy exit, even stepping into an elevator if the doors hesitate can make her feel the metal door of the shed again and hear her niece’s voice. She has started leaving doors propped open when she can, and if a room feels close or difficult to get out of, she finds a reason not to enter.

The same is true outside. Because the event took place in a wooded natural area, any similar setting has become charged for her. A tree-lined walking path, the smell of damp earth after rain, the sight of park signage at the edge of a preserve can bring the scene back so vividly that she has to turn around. She no longer accepts invitations to picnics or outdoor gatherings in unfamiliar parks. It is not only that such places remind her of what happened; she has become convinced that in unfamiliar places she cannot properly judge what danger may be waiting, and that once something goes wrong she will again be unable to stop it. She plans routes carefully, avoids detours, and keeps to locations she knows well enough to map exits in her head.

Her work has narrowed around these fears. As an auditor, she used to travel to offices she had never visited and inspect storage areas, file rooms, and back-office spaces. Over the past year she has begun refusing assignments in unfamiliar buildings. When she must go, she scans continuously—doors, locks, stairwells, who is nearby, whether a space feels too isolated. Colleagues have noticed that she asks to keep meeting room doors ajar and becomes visibly tense if someone closes them. On one recent visit, seeing a memorial photo of a deceased employee in a lobby display unexpectedly brought back not only her niece’s face but the unbearable awareness of her as a victim, and Nadia had to leave the building and sit in her car shaking. She has become embarrassed by these episodes and has started limiting face-to-face work when possible, which has strained her standing with her team.

Over time Nadia has come to feel altered in ways that trouble her deeply. She says she has lost faith—in people who say places are safe, in life’s fairness, and in any larger sense that the world is ordered or benevolent. She had once believed that vigilance and responsibility could protect the people she loved; now she is certain bad things can happen without warning and that when they do, she will be helpless. She is also frightened by her own body. Even in settings she knows are safe, it reacts as though danger is present, flooding her with alarm before she can reason with it. At night this leaves her lying awake, listening for sounds, replaying possibilities, or waking suddenly and struggling to settle again.

What finally brought Nadia to seek help was a combination of exhaustion and shame after she panicked during a routine audit in a locked records room and then spent the night awake, convinced she was unraveling. She told the therapist she does not want her world to keep shrinking. She is afraid that if this continues she will stop working altogether and withdraw from everyone, but she is also afraid that the memories will always have the power to overtake her without warning. More than anything, she hopes for some way to be in a room with a closed door, or near trees, or in the presence of loss, and remain in the present rather than feeling herself thrown back into the worst moment of her life.
